message.content:
Aluminum moves heat quickly, but how long a pan stays hot depends on how much heat it has stored, and that comes down mostly to mass. A 10-inch cast-iron skillet weighs about five pounds. A thin 10-inch aluminum pan might weigh one. Aluminum stores roughly twice as much heat per pound as iron, yet five pounds of iron still holds more total heat than one pound of aluminum.

Preheat both pans over medium-high heat and lay two cold steaks in each. The steaks draw heat out of the thin aluminum faster than the burner can replace it. The pan's surface cools, juices pool, and the meat steams instead of browning. The cast iron has more stored heat to give up, so its surface stays hot enough to sear. After you turn off the burner, the skillet also stays warm on the table noticeably longer.

Strictly, this compares a heavy pan with a light one, not iron with aluminum. A thick aluminum pan weighing five pounds would actually store more heat than the cast iron and spread it more evenly across the bottom. Thin pans of either metal tend to run hot directly over the flame, and cast iron does the same.
